name: The Chouf & Beiteddine Palace
tagline: Lebanon's southern mountains: an Ottoman-era palace of courtyards and mosaics, a stone village that was once the emirs' capital, and the country's largest cedar reserve.
highlight: Beiteddine Palace, a huge 19th-century mountain palace of arcaded courtyards, mosaics and gardens, and one of the finest Ottoman-era buildings in the Levant.
shortDescription: A green, terraced mountain region 45 km south-east of Beirut, with Beiteddine Palace, the historic village of Deir al-Qamar, Druze and Christian villages and the Chouf Cedar Reserve.
metaDescription: A Chouf and Beiteddine travel guide: Beiteddine Palace and its mosaics, Deir al-Qamar's old village, the Chouf Cedar Reserve, Druze culture, the summer festival and hiking, with a one-day plan from Beirut.
nearestAirport: Beirut Rafic Hariri (BEY), about 1 hour 15 minutes
knownFor: Beiteddine Palace, Deir al-Qamar, the Chouf Cedar Reserve, Druze villages
goodFor: Mountain scenery, Ottoman architecture, walking, a cool summer day

image.alt: The arcaded courtyard of Beiteddine Palace in the Chouf mountains

intro: The Chouf is the range of terraced mountains south-east of Beirut, rising from the coastal plain to about 2,000 metres. It is the historic heartland of the Druze, a religious community that split from Ismaili Islam in the 11th century, and it has a long Christian, particularly Maronite, presence as well. For centuries the emirs of Mount Lebanon, notably Fakhr al-Din II and Bashir II Shihab, ruled from these hills, and their palaces and villages are the region's great heritage.

The biggest is Beiteddine Palace, built between about 1788 and 1818 by Emir Bashir II Shihab, with a series of courtyards, arcades, fountains, baths, mosaics and painted ceilings on a hilltop. Nearby, the village of Deir al-Qamar, the former capital of the emirs, is a well-preserved stone town of red-tiled roofs and cobbled squares. Above them, the Chouf Cedar Reserve is Lebanon's largest nature reserve, protecting a quarter of the country's remaining cedars.

The Chouf is a peaceful region of orchards, olive groves and villages, and it is a favourite summer escape for people from Beirut. It has been affected less directly by recent conflict than the south, but check your government's advice.

whyVisit.intro: The Chouf is the most scenic and cooling day out from Beirut, and it shows a different side of Lebanon.

points.title: Beiteddine Palace
points.text: A masterpiece of 19th-century Lebanese architecture, with limestone courtyards, Ottoman and Italianate details and one of the largest collections of Byzantine mosaics in the country.

points.title: Deir al-Qamar
points.text: A village of old stone houses, a mosque, a church and a palace that was once the seat of Mount Lebanon's emirs.

points.title: The Chouf Cedar Reserve
points.text: Three groves of ancient cedars, oak and juniper, with marked trails and views over the mountains and the sea.

points.title: Druze culture
points.text: The region is the centre of the Druze community in Lebanon, with villages, shrines and traditions that are distinct.

points.title: A summer festival
points.text: The Beiteddine Art Festival, held in the palace courtyards in summer, features concerts, theatre and dance.

attractionsIntro: The palace and the village are close together, and the reserve is a short drive.

attractions.name: Beiteddine Palace
attractions.text: A hilltop palace built by Emir Bashir Shihab II, with three main courtyards, a harem, baths, a mosque, stables and gardens. It is now a national monument and houses a museum of mosaics and a collection of weapons.
attractions.tip: Allow two hours, and go on a weekday morning.

attractions.name: The Beiteddine Mosaic Museum
attractions.text: A museum in the palace displaying Byzantine mosaics from Jiyeh and other sites, including a well-known scene of the cycle of life.
attractions.tip: Visit before the tour groups arrive.

attractions.name: Deir al-Qamar

image.alt: Stone houses and cobbled lanes in the village of Deir al-Qamar

attractions.text: A stone village 5 km from Beiteddine, with a main square, the Fakhreddine Mosque, the Palace of Youssef Shehab and a Maronite church. It is one of the best-preserved historic villages in Lebanon.
attractions.tip: Walk around the square and lanes, and have coffee.

attractions.name: The Chouf Cedar Reserve

image.alt: Snow-covered cedars in the Chouf Cedar Reserve

attractions.text: A protected area of about 550 km² that covers a large part of the southern mountains, with cedar groves at Maaser el Chouf, Barouk and Ain Zhalta. Marked trails, guesthouses and a visitor centre help walkers.
attractions.tip: Go in spring or autumn, and check trail conditions.

attractions.name: Moukhtara Palace
attractions.text: The seat of the Jumblatt family, one of the leading Druze families, with a palace and gardens in a village near Beiteddine. It is usually closed to the public.
attractions.tip: It can be seen from the road.

attractions.name: The Barouk Cedar Forest
attractions.text: One of the largest cedar groves in Lebanon, in the reserve, with walking trails.

attractions.name: Druze villages
attractions.text: Villages such as Niha, Baakleen and Mukhtara have shrines, old houses and a distinct religious culture. The Druze faith is secretive, and visitors are welcomed at some sites.

thingsToDoIntro: The Chouf is a place for a relaxed day of walking and looking.

thingsToDo.title: Tour Beiteddine Palace
thingsToDo.text: Walk through the courtyards, the baths and the museum, and enjoy the views.

thingsToDo.title: Walk in Deir al-Qamar
thingsToDo.text: Stroll around the square and old lanes, and stop at the cafés.

thingsToDo.title: Hike in the cedar reserve
thingsToDo.text: Follow marked trails through cedar groves and along the ridge, with views to the Mediterranean.
thingsToDo.tip: Take water, and wear sturdy shoes.

thingsToDo.title: Have lunch in a mountain village
thingsToDo.text: Restaurants serve mezze and grills on terraces with mountain views.

thingsToDo.title: Attend the Beiteddine Art Festival
thingsToDo.text: Concerts and performances in the palace courtyards during summer, when held.
thingsToDo.tip: Check the programme and book tickets.

thingsToDo.title: Combine with Sidon
thingsToDo.text: Sidon is about 40 minutes from Beiteddine, and the two make a full day.
thingsToDo.tip: Start in the mountains and finish on the coast.

foodIntro: Chouf cooking is mountain cooking: grilled meats, mezze, fruit and preserves, and specialities of the Druze villages.

foods.name: Mezze
foods.text: Salads, dips, kibbeh and pastries, often with local olive oil.
foods.whereToTry: Restaurants in Deir al-Qamar and Beiteddine.

foods.name: Grilled meats
foods.text: Lamb and chicken cooked over charcoal, served with garlic sauce.

foods.name: Mountain fruit
foods.text: Apples, cherries, figs and grapes grown in the terraces, sold fresh and as jams.

foods.name: Olive oil and soap
foods.text: The Chouf produces olive oil and traditional soap.

foods.name: Manakish
foods.text: Flatbread with za'atar, cheese or meat.

foods.name: Sweets and coffee
foods.text: Traditional sweets and strong coffee in the village cafés.

accommodation.intro: Most visitors visit as a day trip from Beirut, but guesthouses in the villages and the reserve are a pleasant option.

areas.name: Deir al-Qamar and Beiteddine
areas.text: Small hotels and guesthouses in restored stone houses.

areas.name: The cedar reserve villages
areas.text: Guesthouses in Ain Zhalta, Maaser el Chouf and Barouk run in partnership with the reserve.

gettingThere.intro: Beiteddine is about 45 km south-east of Beirut by winding mountain roads.

options.text: About 1 hour 15 minutes from Beirut without traffic. The road climbs from the coast.
Shared taxis run from Beirut's Cola station to Beiteddine and Deir al-Qamar.
Day tours from Beirut often include Beiteddine, Deir al-Qamar and the cedars.

gettingAround.intro: A car or driver is the easiest way to link the palace, the village and the reserve.

options.text: Roads link the villages, though they are narrow and winding.
Deir al-Qamar and the palace grounds are walkable, and trails link the villages in the reserve.
Local taxis take you between villages.

bestTime.headline: April–June and September–October
bestTime.summary: The Chouf is at 800–1,900 m and is cooler than the coast. Spring and autumn are best for walking, and summer is a pleasant escape.

seasons.text: Green hills and wildflowers, with snow on the peaks until April.
Warm and dry, with cool evenings and the Beiteddine festival.
Warm and clear, with autumn colours.
Cold and often snowy, with few visitors. Higher roads can close.

bestTime.avoid: Snowstorms in winter, and August weekends.

itinerary.title: One day in the Chouf
itinerary.intro: Beiteddine Palace in the morning, lunch in Deir al-Qamar, a walk in the cedar reserve in the afternoon.

days.title: Palace, village and cedars
days.summary: A scenic day in the mountains.
days.morning: Beiteddine Palace and its mosaic museum.
days.afternoon: Lunch in Deir al-Qamar, then the Chouf Cedar Reserve.
days.evening: Drive back to Beirut or on to Sidon.

tipsIntro: The Chouf is easy, and a few tips help.
tips: Go on a weekday. Weekends and summer evenings are busy with Lebanese visitors.
Check whether the palace is open, and confirm festival dates if you want to attend.
Dress modestly in the villages and religious sites.
Bring a jacket and walking shoes for the reserve.
Hire a driver. The roads are narrow and winding.
Bring cash, as small shops may not take cards.
Respect Druze customs, and ask before entering religious places.

faq.a: A 19th-century palace built by Emir Bashir II Shihab, with courtyards, baths and a museum of mosaics. It is one of the best examples of Lebanese architecture of the period.
A religious community that emerged in the 11th century from Ismaili Islam, and is centred in Lebanon, Syria, Israel and Jordan. Their beliefs are known only to initiated members.

faq.q: How long do you need in the Chouf?
faq.a: One day covers the palace, the village and a short walk. Two days let you hike and stay in a guesthouse.

faq.q: Is the Chouf safe to visit?
faq.a: It has been less affected by recent conflict than the south, but conditions in Lebanon can change quickly. Check your government's advice.

faq.q: What is the Chouf Cedar Reserve?
faq.a: Lebanon's largest nature reserve, protecting about a quarter of the country's remaining cedar forest, together with oak, juniper and wildlife.
It has traditionally been held in summer, usually July and August. Dates vary and the festival has been suspended in difficult years, so check.
